title: SYSK Selects: How The Enlightenment Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun-style episode in which Josh and Chuck explore the Enlightenment as a broad, ongoing intellectual shift from religious dogma and monarchy toward reason, science, humanism, empiricism, and democracy. They trace precursors (Dark Ages scholasticism, Gutenberg's printing press, the translation of Aristotle, the Renaissance and humanism, Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, Bacon's scientific method, Descartes), key Enlightenment thinkers (Locke, Hume, Rousseau, Montesquieu, Voltaire, Adam Smith, Kant), the salons, enlightened despots, the American and French revolutions and the Reign of Terror, Romanticism as a reaction, and debates about colonialism and whether the Enlightenment still continues today, including the Bill Maher and Ben Affleck argument. The episode ends with listener mail about a mad cow and mummy fertilizer theory.

segments.title: Josh introduces the Selects pick
segments.summary: Josh explains why he chose the Enlightenment episode, arguing the rationalism versus superstition divide still shapes world politics. The hosts open the show.

segments.title: Enlightenment as an ongoing debate
segments.summary: The hosts say the Enlightenment is still being argued over, citing the Bill Maher and Ben Affleck exchange about Islam as an example of moral absolutism versus moral relativism. They note the Enlightenment was many changes at once: religious, political and economic, across many countries.

segments.title: Precursors: Newton, Thirty Years War, Dark Ages
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Isaac Newton and the falling apple, David Hume's skepticism about it, the Thirty Years War and its effect on church and state allegiance, and how the so-called Dark Ages are a disparaging label, with scholasticism and Roger Bacon's work.

segments.title: Printing press, Aristotle, humanism and Renaissance
segments.summary: The hosts cover Gutenberg's printing press in 1438, the translation of Aristotle into Latin, Leonardo Bruni reviving humanism after Petrarch, and the Renaissance's focus on human ability.

segments.title: Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo and the Church
segments.summary: The hosts describe Copernicus's infinite universe against Aristotle's crystal spheres, Kepler's elliptical orbits against the Church's view of the circle as perfect, and Galileo's recantation. They also mention Bacon as a creator of the scientific method and Descartes's mind-matter ideas.

segments.title: Social contract, Locke and natural rights
segments.summary: The hosts explain the social contract idea from Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau, in which people give up some natural rights, including retribution, to the state's monopoly on violence. They also cover Locke's tabula rasa and nurture over nature.

segments.title: Voltaire, the salons and the philosophes
segments.summary: The hosts describe Voltaire's exile in England, his return to France, and the private salons where radical ideas were discussed. They name the philosophes, the Church's hostility, deism and the clockmaker God, and Montesquieu's separation of powers.

segments.title: Regional Enlightenments and Adam Smith
segments.summary: The hosts note the French emphasis on the arts and the English on science and economics. They cover Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations and laissez-faire, and David Hume's empiricism and cause and effect, including the sun-rising example.

segments.title: Enlightened rulers, Kant and revolutions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Catherine the Great and Frederick the Great hosting philosophes, Kant's motto dare to know and categorical imperative, and then the American Revolution versus the French Revolution, Robespierre and the Reign of Terror.

segments.title: Aftermath: Romanticism, colonialism and modern debates
segments.summary: The hosts say the French Revolution's chaos was blamed on the Enlightenment and Romanticism followed. They discuss critiques that Enlightenment thought supported colonialism, Jonathan Israel's argument about Spinoza, and Anthony Pagden's view that the project continues.

segments.title: Further reading and closing discussion
segments.summary: The hosts recommend articles and books, including Tim O'Neil's work on the Dark Ages myth, and say the period is a time of change.

segments.title: Listener mail: mad cow and mummy fertilizer theory
segments.summary: A listener from Seattle, Darren Gray, proposes that ground-up Egyptian mummies used as fertilizer could have spread prions to cows and caused mad cow disease. The hosts invite listener responses and sign off.
